name: Gareth Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a pig and arable farm run by two brothers, the Mercers. We've got 600 sows indoors and about 400 acres of wheat and barley, and a lot of the barley goes back into the pigs as feed. My day starts at six in the farrowing house, which is where the sows have their piglets, checking every litter, then weaning, washing pens, and moving pigs. In spring and harvest I'm on the tractor or helping with the grain dryer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use AI tools a lot. Where do they fit in?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I ask a chat app to check feed sums, I've got an app on my phone that listens to the pig sheds and flags coughing before you'd hear it, and I built Rob Mercer a spreadsheet for the grain stores. I'm still not great at the hands-on stuff, the older lads are quicker at everything with a pig, so the tech is where I can be useful. I live in a flat above the village shop with my dog, Biscuit, and I'm always the one my mates ring when their phone breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that'd be a bit of a let-down for me. I'm one of the people who thinks it could actually make farming less brutal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because there was real good in it, catching sick pigs early, using less spray. I'd still post about the stuff that does work, the cough-listening app and the grain sensors. Somebody has to keep the faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd also be a bit relieved for the older lads like Pete, who's been here thirty years and hates screens. And I'd know that if nothing changes, I stay the junior who's slow with a sow and quick with a phone, which is not a career. If AI goes bust, I'm just the lad who fixes the Wi-Fi in the pig shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at the Mercers' and keep pushing the small tools that work, maybe sensors in the grain stores. I'd probably start helping other farms around here set up apps and sensors on a Saturday, for a bit of extra cash. And I'd put some money by, I've got about three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little bored. Disappointed, I guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the Mercers pay for the extra tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob would, if I showed him the numbers. Phil, the other brother, would say his dad never needed a sensor. They'd argue about it for a month and then buy half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does Pete matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He taught me to handle a sow without getting crushed, and he's never once made me feel stupid. He's 61 and he'd hate any of this. If the tech does arrive, I want it to make his back hurt less, not get him sacked.

S0.say: I'd say it's a shame because the tools could have done real good, like catching sick pigs early and using less spray. I'd keep posting about the small things that work.
S0.think: I'd be relieved for older workers who hate screens, but for me it means staying the junior who's slow with a sow and quick with a phone. That's not a career.
S0.do: Keeps working on the pig and arable farm and pushes small tools like grain store sensors. Starts helping neighbouring farms set up apps and sensors on Saturdays for extra cash, and keeps adding to about three months of savings.
S0.feel: Calm, a little bored and disappointed.
S0.quote: If AI goes bust, I'm just the lad who fixes the Wi-Fi in the pig shed.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth is the rare farmer who'd be disappointed by the plateau, because the tech is where he's useful. He worries about an older colleague, Pete, more than himself. Even in the calmest scenario he'd start a small side business helping other farms with sensors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the one I'm half expecting. And I'd want to be in the middle of it, not watching from the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be brilliant if workers get a share of it. Robots doing the washing and the heavy lifting, people doing the stockmanship. I'd be online saying it, and I'd also be saying the gains shouldn't all go to the people who own the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's my chance. The Mercers will need someone who can run the robots and talk to the software, and right now that's me. But I'd also feel guilty, because the jobs that shrink would be Pete's and the lads who do pen washing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push Rob to trial a pen-washing robot and the camera system that weighs pigs from above, and volunteer to run them. Sign up for the evening course at the agricultural college on farm technology, I'd pay for it myself if I had to. And I'd ask the brothers, before any robot arrives, to keep Pete on doing the jobs it can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly excited. With a little knot about Pete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the brothers said no to keeping Pete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd argue, but I'm 27 and the junior, so they wouldn't listen much. I'd be the one installing the robot that does Pete's job. I'd hate that, and I'd still do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talk about workers getting a share. What would that look like here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bonus tied to what the robots save, or a group of us owning a robot together and hiring it out. There's a machinery ring round here already, farmers sharing kit. Why not a robot ring that the workers have a stake in?

S1.say: I'd say this could be brilliant if workers get a share: robots doing the heavy lifting and people doing the stockmanship. The gains shouldn't all go to whoever owns the machines.
S1.think: It's my chance, because the farm will need someone who can run robots and software, and that's me. I'd feel guilty that the jobs shrinking are my older colleague's.
S1.do: Pushes the owners to trial a pen-washing robot and a camera weighing system, and volunteers to run them. Signs up for an evening farm technology course, paying himself if needed, and asks the owners to keep his older colleague on.
S1.feel: Mostly excited and calm, with a knot of worry about his colleague.
S1.quote: I'd be the one installing the robot that does Pete's job. I'd hate that, and I'd still do it.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth's say and think line up on the tech but split on the people: publicly he talks about sharing the gains, privately he admits he'd install the robot that replaces his mentor. His progressive instinct shows up as ideas for worker-owned machinery. He'd act first and argue later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. Even I'd struggle with that, and I'm the one who likes this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for public ownership, or at least for the public getting a cut. If machines can do all the work, the people who own them can't keep all of it. I'd be marching, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, being good with the tech buys me about a year. I'd be installing robots on every farm in the county for twelve months and then there'd be robots installing robots. Being quick with tech just gets me to the front of the queue. It's still the same queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quit the Mercers' and get a job with one of the robot firms setting kit up on farms, because that's where the money would be for a short window. Save every bit of the extra pay, aiming for a year of bills. And get involved in whatever campaign is pushing for a basic income or a share of robot profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited for about a week, then anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel installing robots on farms you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rotten, on some of them. I'd be walking into yards where I know the lads, setting up the machine that sends them home. I'd try to be honest with them about what it does, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Biscuit and the flat, the life you've got here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the thing. A robot firm would have me driving all over the country, so I'd probably keep the flat and get my mum to have Biscuit half the week. I'm not attached to the job, but I'm attached to this village.

S2.say: I'd say this is the moment for public ownership, or at least a public cut, because the machine owners can't keep everything. I'd be marching and mean it.
S2.think: Being good with tech buys me about a year before robots install robots. It only gets me to the front of the same queue.
S2.do: Leaves the farm for a job with a robot firm installing kit on farms, and saves the extra pay toward a year of bills. Joins campaigns for a basic income or a public share of robot profits.
S2.feel: Excited for about a week, then anxious.
S2.quote: Being quick with tech just gets me to the front of the queue. It's still the same queue.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most adaptive farmer sees that skill with tech only buys a short window when AGI arrives fast. Gareth would grab that window for money while campaigning for public ownership, which he doesn't see as a contradiction. His tie to the village is stronger than his tie to the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to ride it for a while, I reckon. You can surf a wave you see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's use the time to make sure it's shared. I'd be talking up local co-ops that own the robots, so the money stays in villages like ours. And I'd be telling every young farmer I know to learn the kit now, while it still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well for three or four years, then hit the same wall as everyone. The difference is I'd have savings and maybe a stake in something. Five years doesn't save the job, but it lets me build a raft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay at the Mercers' a year and run every bit of new kit, then go to a robot firm or set up on my own fitting and fixing machines. Put money into a local co-op if we got one going, that's my idea of investing. And save hard, at least a third of what I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said build a raft. What's on the raft?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings, a share in a co-op that owns the machines, and mates. If the co-op owns ten robots and hires them to farms, the profit comes back to the people in it. If the robots are coming either way, I'd rather own a bit of one than be replaced by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Pete be in that co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want him in it, even if he never touches a screen. He knows more about pigs than any robot will for a while. The co-op could pay him to teach the machines, or to check on them.

S3.say: I'd say let's use the time to make sure it's shared, with local co-ops owning the robots so money stays in the villages. I'd tell every young farmer to learn the kit while it still pays.
S3.think: I'd do well for three or four years and then hit the same wall as everyone, but with savings and a stake in something. Five years doesn't save the job, but it lets me build a raft.
S3.do: Stays a year on the farm running new kit, then moves to a robot firm or sets up fitting and fixing machines himself. Buys into a local robot co-op and saves at least a third of his earnings.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: If the robots are coming either way, I'd rather own a bit of one than be replaced by one.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Gareth shifts from grabbing short-term pay to building ownership, which he calls a raft. He'd rather own a share of a robot than be replaced by one, and he'd bring his older colleague into it. His politics and his career plan merge in the co-op idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to do it properly, and long enough to get lazy, which is the danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a ten-year chance to set things up fairly, and I'd be pushing for it everywhere. Robot co-ops, retraining money, a share of profits for every community. I'd probably sound like a broken record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry I'd coast for five years because I'm doing well with the tech, and then wake up at 35 with nothing built. Adaptable people can get comfy too. I'd have to make myself do the hard bits early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go to college properly, maybe a part-time degree in agricultural engineering, starting next year. Set up the robot co-op with a few mates in year two or three as a side business. And keep a slice of savings invested, not just sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More hopeful than the others, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you not coast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing it down, honestly, a plan for each year, and a mate who checks it. My mum's good at that, she'd ask me every Sunday. Ten years is enough time to get it right and plenty of time to forget you're supposed to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two- and five-year pictures, what does the extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'd sell my skills fast and hope. With five I'd build a raft. With ten I could build something that lasts after the robots arrive, like the co-op, and get a qualification that means something. More time helps me more than most, I think, because I'll actually use it.

S4.say: I'd say it's a ten-year chance to set things up fairly, with robot co-ops, retraining money and a share of profits for every community. I'd sound like a broken record.
S4.think: I worry I'd coast for five years because I'm doing well with the tech, then wake up at 35 with nothing built. Adaptable people can get comfortable too.
S4.do: Starts a part-time degree in agricultural engineering next year and sets up a robot co-op with friends as a side business in year two or three. Keeps part of his savings invested rather than sitting idle.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than in the faster scenarios.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to get it right and plenty of time to forget you're supposed to.
S4.fieldNote: Gareth sees the risk of complacency in himself, which was unexpected from such a keen adopter. He mapped clearly how warning time changes his plan: sell skills fast, build a raft, or build something lasting. He's the one person who says more time helps him because he'll use it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, not for me so much, but because there'd be no time to set up anything fair, the co-ops, the profit share. It would all just go to whoever owns the robots on day one. What would help is a law that gives communities and workers a share of what the machines earn, and cheap loans for co-ops to buy them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who owns the data. Every sensor on that farm is learning from what Pete and I do, and we're the ones teaching the machine that replaces us. Nobody pays us for that.

headlineQuote: Being quick with tech just gets me to the front of the queue. It's still the same queue.
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old junior on a pig and arable farm who lives alone with his dog above the village shop and uses AI tools every day. He's still slow with the animals but quick with sensors and spreadsheets, and he leans left, with a strong belief that workers should share in what machines earn. He'd be disappointed by the plateau, excited by steady disruption, and sobered by the fast AGI scenario, where he sees that being quick with tech only puts him at the front of the same queue. With more warning time he'd build ownership through a local robot co-op and a degree, though he fears getting comfortable. Throughout, he worries about his older mentor Pete.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because there'd be no time to set up co-ops or profit sharing and everything would go to whoever owns the robots on day one.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving workers and communities a share of what machines earn, and cheap loans for co-ops to buy robots.
